title: Short Stuff: Ivar The Boneless
summary: Short Stuff episode on Ivar the Boneless, the Viking leader often linked to the Great Heathen Army. Josh and Chuck contrast the History Channel's Vikings portrayal (Ivar as a leader who could not use his legs) with the historical record. They cover how Vikings were written about by their victims, the violence of the medieval era generally, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and Annals of Ulster mentions of Ivar (who may be the same man, dying in 873 per the Annals of Ulster is not stated; the transcript says eighty three), the Icelandic sagas where the boneless nickname first appears, and a proposed Latin transcription error (exos meaning boneless versus exosus meaning detestable) that could mean his nickname was "the hated" rather than "the boneless."

segments.title: Opening banter and Vikings mushrooms joke
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with jokes about Vikings and berserker mode, mention the upcoming Robert Eggers Viking movie, and introduce Ivar the Boneless as he appears in the History Channel's Vikings series.

segments.title: Vikings as written by their victims
segments.summary: The hosts argue that most surviving accounts of Vikings were written by their enemies and victims, and that the Vikings were not more violent than other medieval peoples. They cite Charlemagne ordering the beheading of Saxons as an example of violence elsewhere.

segments.title: Great Heathen Army and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
segments.summary: The Great Heathen Army is described as a loose group of Scandinavian armies that invaded the British Isles over more than a decade. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle mentions the Great Army and the brother of Ivar, and so Ivar by extension.

segments.title: Annals of Ulster and identity of Ivar
segments.summary: The Annals of Ulster record a Viking named Ivar or Emar, king of the Northmen in Britain and Ireland, who died in 83 (as stated). Historians think this is probably the same Ivar, though it is not certain.

segments.title: Icelandic sagas and origin of the boneless nickname
segments.summary: The Icelandic sagas, transcribed in the thirteenth century, are described as novelistic narratives that likely exaggerate. They are where the boneless nickname first appears. The hosts suggest 'legless' might have been a transcription mix-up.

segments.title: Latin transcription error theory: exos vs exosus
segments.summary: The hosts describe a theory that medieval copyists confused exos (boneless) with exosus (detestable), so the nickname may have meant hated rather than boneless. Historians think the History Channel's version is doubtful, though possible.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about the time machine and wrap up the short episode, with a note about the show's production by iHeartRadio.
